blocks.text: A thermistor signal is smoothed by a simple resistor and capacitor before it reaches a data logger. Step the temperature suddenly and the logger's reading does not jump; it creeps up to the new value along a smooth curve. How long the creep lasts is set by one number, the time constant, and every first-order circuit in mechatronics, from sensor filters to motor coils, shares the same curve.

blocks.markdown: A circuit with **one** energy-storage element (a capacitor or an inductor) and resistors is a **first-order circuit**. Following a sudden change, such as a switch closing, the stored quantity cannot jump (capacitor voltage and inductor current are continuous). It moves exponentially from its initial value to its final (steady-state) value. The speed of that movement is set by the **time constant** $\tau$.

blocks.title: Time constant
blocks.text: For a capacitor $C$ charging through a resistance $R$, $\tau=RC$. For an inductor $L$ in series with a resistance $R$, $\tau=L/R$. In both cases $\tau$ is in seconds and $R$ is the Thevenin resistance seen by the storage element.

blocks.caption: General first-order response: V_0 is the initial value, V_f the final value after a long time, t measured from the switching instant

blocks.markdown: For a capacitor charged from 0 V by a step of size $V_s$, $V_0=0$ and $V_f=V_s$, so $v_C=V_s(1-e^{-t/\tau})$. At $t=\tau$ the voltage has covered $1-e^{-1}=63.2\%$ of the step; at $2\tau$, 86.5 %; at $3\tau$, 95.0 %; at $5\tau$, 99.3 %. For an inductor driven by a step, the current $i_L$ has the same shape with $I_f=V_s/R$.

blocks.title: Capacitor voltage after a step
blocks.prompt: A 5.0 V step is applied to a series 47 k$\Omega$ resistor and 2.2 uF capacitor (initially uncharged). Find $\tau$ and the capacitor voltage 150 ms after the step.
blocks.answer: tau = 103 ms; after 150 ms the capacitor voltage is 3.83 V, about 77 % of the final value.

blocks.markdown: **Settling time.** Rearranging the charging equation gives the time to reach any voltage $v$: $t=\tau\ln\dfrac{V_f-V_0}{V_f-v}$. For 95 % of the final value, $V_f-v=0.05\,(V_f-V_0)$, so $t_{95}=\tau\ln 20=2.996\,\tau\approx3\tau$. Engineers often take $3\tau$ as the time to reach 95 % and $5\tau$ as 'settled'.

blocks.caption: Time to reach a chosen value and the 95 % settling time

blocks.title: An RL circuit
blocks.prompt: A coil of $L=0.30$ H and total series resistance $R=15\ \Omega$ is connected to a 12 V supply at $t=0$. Find $\tau$, the final current and the time to reach 95 % of it.

steps.text: Final current (inductor is a short at DC steady state).

blocks.answer: tau = 20 ms, final current 0.80 A, 95 % (0.76 A) reached after about 60 ms.

blocks.caption: Rise of a first-order step response (for decay, the remaining column is the value left)

items: $\tau=RC$ or $L/R$ in seconds; bigger R or C (or L, smaller R for RL) means slower response.
Discharge from $V_0$ to zero follows $v=V_0e^{-t/\tau}$: 36.8 % left after one $\tau$.
The tangent at $t=0$ would reach the final value in exactly one $\tau$.
The same $\tau$ governs charging and discharging through the same resistance.

blocks.title: Find the right R
blocks.text: $R$ in $\tau$ is the resistance the storage element drives or is driven through, the Thevenin resistance seen at its terminals, not simply 'the resistor in the picture'.

points: Time constant is $\tau=RC$ for RC circuits and $\tau=L/R$ for RL circuits.
Response: $v=V_f+(V_0-V_f)e^{-t/\tau}$; after one $\tau$ it has covered 63.2 % of the change.
95 % of the final value is reached at $\tau\ln20\approx3\tau$.

questions.stem: What is the time constant of a series circuit of a 10 k$\Omega$ resistor and a 100 nF capacitor?

distractorRationale.b: Wrong: this mistakes 100 nF for 100 uF.
distractorRationale.c: Wrong: this loses a factor of 10 in the product.
distractorRationale.d: Wrong: this gains a factor of 10 in the product.

questions.explanation: $\tau=RC=10\times10^{3}\times100\times10^{-9}=1.0\times10^{-3}$ s, or 1.0 ms. Convert nanofarads to farads before multiplying.

questions.stem: A 50 mH inductor is in series with a total resistance of 25 ohm. What is the time constant?

distractorRationale.b: Wrong: this multiplies L by R instead of dividing.
distractorRationale.c: Wrong: this divides R by L.

questions.explanation: For an RL circuit $\tau=L/R=0.050/25=0.002$ s = 2.0 ms. Larger inductance slows the current build-up; larger resistance speeds it.

questions.stem: Approximately how many time constants must elapse for a first-order step response to reach 95 % of its final value?

distractorRationale.c: Wrong: five tau reaches about 99.3 %, the 'settled' convention.

questions.explanation: Setting $1-e^{-t/\tau}=0.95$ gives $t/\tau=\ln20=2.996$. Hence three time constants give 95 %.

questions.stem: A 12 V step is applied to an uncharged 1.0 uF capacitor in series with 22 k$\Omega$. What is the capacitor voltage 30 ms after the step?

distractorRationale.b: Wrong: this is the decay value 12 e^(-t/tau), the voltage still remaining to be charged.
distractorRationale.c: Wrong: this is the voltage at exactly one tau (63.2 %), not at 30 ms.
distractorRationale.d: Wrong: this is the final value, reached only after several time constants.

questions.stem: A capacitor charged to 9.0 V is discharged through a resistor. At a time equal to one time constant after the switch closes, what is its voltage?

distractorRationale.b: Wrong: this is 9 x 0.632, the charging fraction applied to a discharge.
distractorRationale.c: Wrong: the capacitor has not fully discharged after one tau.
distractorRationale.d: Wrong: this assumes a linear fall to half at one tau.

questions.explanation: Discharge follows $v=V_0e^{-t/\tau}$, so at $t=\tau$ the voltage is $9.0\times0.3679=3.31$ V. 36.8 % of the initial voltage remains.

questions.stem: A 3.3 k$\Omega$ resistor charges a 47 uF capacitor. What is the time constant, in milliseconds?
A solenoid has $L=120$ mH and a series resistance of 40 ohm, and is switched onto a DC supply. How long (in ms) does the current take to reach 95 % of its final value?
A 5.0 V step is applied to a 10 k$\Omega$ resistor in series with an uncharged 0.47 uF capacitor. How long (in ms) does the capacitor voltage take to reach 4.0 V?
Explain physically why the time constant of an RC circuit increases when either R or C is increased, and what 'one time constant' means for the response.
markingGuide: Larger C needs more charge to reach the same voltage
Larger R reduces the charging current for a given voltage difference
Both slow the rate of voltage change so tau = RC increases
One tau is the time to complete 63.2 % of the total change (or time for decay to 36.8 %)
Equivalent statement: initial slope would reach the final value in one tau
questions.explanation: Charging a capacitor to a given voltage needs a charge $Q=CV$, so a larger $C$ requires more charge, while a larger $R$ reduces the current $i=(V_s-v)/R$ delivering that charge. Both slow the process, which is why $\tau=RC$ grows with each. After one time constant the capacitor has completed 63.2 % of its voltage change.

questions.stem: A 12-bit ADC input (full scale 3.3 V) is preceded by an RC filter with $R=1.0$ k$\Omega$ and $C=10$ uF. After a full-scale step at the input, estimate how long the designer must wait before sampling so that the capacitor voltage is within one LSB of final. Show the reasoning.
markingGuide: One LSB = 3.3/4096 = 0.806 mV, so remaining fraction = 1/4096
Sets e^(-t/tau) = 1/4096, giving t = tau ln 4096
Notes this is about 8.3 time constants, much longer than the 3 tau used for 95 %
questions.explanation: The time constant is $\tau=RC=1.0\times10^3\times10\times10^{-6}=10$ ms. Being within one LSB means a remaining error of $1/4096$ of the step, so $e^{-t/\tau}=1/4096$ and $t=\tau\ln4096=10\times8.32=83.2$ ms. Higher accuracy therefore needs many more time constants than the 95 % rule of thumb.
